item.title: Stop Saying “I Can’t Afford It” to Your Adult Child
item.description:
Parenting

Stop Saying “I Can’t Afford It” to Your Adult Child

Saying "I can't afford it" may counterintuitively weaken your financial boundary

Posted August 21, 2026

Key points
  • "I can't afford" it can turn a boundary you are trying to set into a debate you don't want.
  • Just because you have the money doesn't mean you "should" give it or that it will truly help your adult child.
  • Remember that your support can build independence but your repeated rescuing can undermine it.

If you are reading this post and are perplexed by the title, you are probably thinking either I flipped my rocker (yep, for me, being an old boomer, that saying lives on), or you straight-up despise the title, or maybe you are intrigued by it. To be clear about why I chose this article’s title, many of my parent-coaching clients share how they rely (unsuccessfully) on the phrase “I can’t afford it” when responding to their adult child’s repeated requests for financial support.

Okay, I get that some parents may be saying, but Dr. Jeff, you don’t get it: I really can’t afford it. I’m a psychologist, not an accountant, and how much money you have in your accounts is not my business, and actually it is not even the point of this post. What I do want to discuss is how these frequently relied-on four words (“I can’t afford it”) end up getting more parents than you could believe to end up opening up their money transfer apps or checkbooks, when deep down they know doing so only provides temporary relief to the long-term problem of their adult children’s lack of understanding of the value of the dollar.

Why I Can’t Afford It Frequently Becomes a Debate

I can’t say I have seen it all, but I have seen a lot when it comes to parents letting their anxiety get in the way of setting financial boundaries with their adult children. For example, when an adult child asks for rent, a car payment, credit card debt, groceries, or yet another emergency, and you respond with “I can’t afford it,” you may be unwittingly setting yourself and your adult child up for a wickedly stressful debate.

I hear firsthand accounts of rebuttals such as, “I just need two thousand to get caught up, and then I’ll pay you back,” or “C’mon, this makes no sense you helped me last time,” or “Don’t tell me you can’t afford it becasue you just went on that expensive vacation and this is for me to have a roof over my head and eat” (I love that one). Consequently, the parents who reach out to me and hear such rebuttals feel desperate and worn down, then feel compelled to give out that money because “I can’t afford it” gets besieged by waves of guilt, and they give in.

Welcome to the Rescue Trap

In my new book, The Rescue Trap: How Well-Meaning Parents Keep Their Adult Children Stuck, I explain that the trap, per se, comes from parents feeling worried or guilty, and that leads them to step in. Let me say something quickly here that I have said in many of my other articles. I am not against parents helping their adult children financially as long as their adult children understand the value of a dollar and have decent overall awareness of what it takes to manage their money. But when you repeatedly rescue your adult child financially, then you are sending a message (like it or not) to your adult child which is: “I’m not sure you can manage money and handle your life without me.” That message, by the way, is not a financial confidence booster, to say the least.

Your Bank Balance Is Not the Boundary

When parents who work with me get to the point of saying something like, “Dr. Jeff, I could give them the money they want, but I really am not comfortable doing it,” I know we are making progress in helping them see the picture more accurately. Because when these parents can flip to “I’m not comfortable paying for that,” or even “I’m not willing to pay for that,” it feels very different to them from “I can’t afford it.” To spell it out, when you say, “I can’t afford it,” you are using circumstances to make the decision for you, but when you say, “I’m not comfortable paying that,” you, as the parent, are making the decision.

What to Say Instead of “I Can’t Afford It”

In closing, I suggest you stop saying, “I can’t afford it.” Instead, try saying something like, “I love you, and I get that this is stressful. But I am not willing to jump in and pay for this because I think you will feel better by problem-solving this for yourself. I’m willing to be a sounding board and help you think through what you can do next to improve your financial situation.”

Yes, for sure, your adult child may not like you saying you won’t put on your financial miracle-worker or first-responder uniform. So, let them have their feelings, because one of the best shifts I see is parents realizing they can love their adult children without literally purchasing relief from their struggles.
